content: Bunium persicum, commonly known as black cumin, is a plant belonging to the Apiaceae family. The dried fruits of Bunium persicum are utilized as a culinary spice in regions such as Northern India, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, and Iran. Locally, it is referred to as kala jeera or shahi jeera in Hindi, translating to black cumin and imperial cumin, respectively. In Persian, it is called zireh kuhi, meaning wild cumin, and in Tajiki, it is known as siyoh dona, meaning black seed. Outside these regions, the spice is virtually unknown and should not be confused with Nigella sativa, which is also often referred to as black cumin. In Bengali, the term kalo jeera refers to Nigella sativa, not Bunium persicum. While Nigella sativa is widely used in Bengali cuisine, Bunium persicum is rare in that context. The plant grows naturally across a broad range, from southeastern Europe to southern Asia. It typically reaches a height of approximately 60 cm and a width of 25 cm. The plant features finely divided leaves and hermaphroditic flowers, which are pollinated by insects and are self-fertile. Its small, rounded taproot is edible, either raw or cooked, and is said to have a flavor reminiscent of sweet chestnuts. The leaves can be used as a herb or garnish, similar to parsley. There is some debate among experts as to whether Bunium persicum is the same species as Bunium bulbocastanum, as both share similar characteristics and uses. Medicinal Applications of Black Cumin (Bunium persicum) Healing Properties The fruit of Bunium persicum is a rich source of thymol, a compound with significant medicinal properties. Thymol is used as an anthelmintic to combat hookworm infections and as an antiseptic in various pharmaceutical formulations. It also acts as a stimulant, promoting diuresis (increased urine production) and alleviating flatulence. Additionally, it enhances stomach function and helps control bleeding. Digestive Disorders Cumin seeds are highly effective in treating digestive issues such as biliousness, morning sickness, indigestion, atonic dyspepsia, diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome, and flatulent colic. A medicinal decoction can be prepared by boiling one teaspoon of cumin seeds in a glass of water, then mixing it with one teaspoon of fresh coriander leaf juice and a pinch of salt. This preparation can be consumed twice daily after meals to alleviate diarrhea. Piles (Hemorrhoids) Black cumin is beneficial in managing piles or hemorrhoids. A mixture of 60 grams of cumin seeds, half of which are roasted, is ground into a flour. Three grams of this flour can be taken with water to provide relief. Insomnia Cumin is effective in addressing sleeplessness. A teaspoon of fried cumin seed powder mixed with the pulp of a ripe banana can be consumed at night to promote sleep. Renal Colic A combination of black cumin seeds, caraway seeds, and black salt is useful in treating renal colic. A mixture of 20 grams of cumin seeds, 12 grams of caraway seeds, and 6 grams of black salt, ground together and mixed with a small amount of vinegar, can be taken in 3-gram doses every hour until relief is achieved. Common Cold Diluted cumin water serves as an antiseptic beverage and is particularly helpful in managing common colds and fevers. To prepare cumin water, a teaspoon of cumin seeds is added to boiling water, simmered briefly, and then allowed to cool. If the cold is accompanied by a sore throat, small pieces of dry ginger can be added to the water to soothe throat irritation. Breast Milk Secretion A decoction of cumin seeds mixed with milk and honey, taken once daily throughout pregnancy, supports the healthy development of the fetus, facilitates childbirth, and enhances breast milk production. Amnesia Cumin seeds are valuable in addressing amnesia or memory dullness. A mixture of three grams of black cumin seeds and 12 grams of pure honey can be consumed to improve memory function. Boils A paste made from black cumin seeds ground in water can be applied to boils, yielding beneficial results. Scorpion Stings A paste prepared from cumin seeds and onion juice can be applied to scorpion stings to reduce the frequency of symptoms. Culinary and Other Uses Cumin seeds are extensively used in spice blends and as a flavoring agent in curries, soups, sausages, bread, and cakes. They are a key ingredient in curry powders, pickles, and chutneys. Additionally, cumin is used in traditional Indian medicine as a carminative. Medicinal Uses of Nigella sativa Nigella sativa, another plant often referred to as black cumin, has been used medicinally for centuries in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. It has been traditionally employed to address a wide range of conditions, including respiratory disorders, gastrointestinal issues, kidney and liver dysfunction, circulatory and immune system support, and general well-being. In Islamic tradition, Nigella sativa is considered one of the most potent healing remedies. Prophet Muhammad is quoted as saying that black seed can cure every disease except death, as documented in the hadith. Ibn Sina, a renowned physician and author of The Canon of Medicine, described Nigella sativa as a seed that invigorates the body and aids in recovery from fatigue and low spirits. It is also listed in the Medicine of the Prophet (Tibb-e-Nabavi) as a remedy for numerous ailments. In the Unani Tibb system of medicine, Nigella sativa is regarded as a valuable treatment for conditions such as asthma, bronchitis, rheumatism, and other inflammatory diseases. It is also used to enhance milk production in nursing mothers, improve digestion, and combat parasitic infections. The oil derived from Nigella sativa is applied to treat skin conditions like eczema and boils, as well as to alleviate cold symptoms. Its extensive range of applications has earned it the Arabic title Habbatul barakah, meaning the seed of blessing.
